module_intro: Before any ICT-specific concept can make sense, a reader needs a precise, mechanical way of describing price movement. Covers swing highs/lows, higher/lower high/low classification, trend, retracement, and key support/resistance levels. Every later module depends on this vocabulary.
prerequisites_stated_in_text: unspecified (book states this module is foundational; 'nothing in the ICT framework needs to be understood before it')
module_objectives: identify a valid swing high and swing low using the three-candle test
classify a swing high as either a higher high or a lower high relative to the prior swing high
classify a swing low as either a higher low or a lower low relative to the prior swing low
determine whether a chart is in an uptrend, downtrend, or range based purely on swing-point sequences
distinguish a normal retracement from a potential trend reversal, and explain why that distinction cannot be made with certainty in real time
mark a key support level and a key resistance level from swing highs/lows that have reacted more than once
explain why swing points are the foundation for every later ICT concept in this book

concepts.name: Swing High
concepts.definition: A price point that is higher than the candles immediately surrounding it, marking a short-term turning point where upward movement paused or reversed.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: A three-candle formation in which the middle candle's high is greater than the high of the candle before it and the high of the candle after it, giving an objective mechanical test. The smallest version is a Short-Term High (STH); it can be promoted to an Intermediate-Term High (ITH) or Long-Term High (LTH) depending on how much structure it governs. This STH/ITH/LTH hierarchy is part of ICT's 'advanced market structure' mapping; not all swing highs carry equal weight.
detection_criteria: Find a candle whose high price is greater than the high of the candle immediately to its left.
Check that the same candle's high price is also greater than the high of the candle immediately to its right.
If both conditions are true, the middle candle qualifies as a swing high (an ICT Short-Term High).
Note the exact price of that candle's high as a reference level for later concepts (liquidity, structure shifts).
Repeat moving left to right across the chart to build a full map of swing highs.
preconditions: unspecified beyond the three-candle test itself
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 105 -> 102 -> 108 -> 104. 105 is a swing high relative to 100 before it and 102 after it. 108 is a larger swing high, higher than 105 and the pullback to 102, and higher than 104 after it; in ICT's hierarchy 108 is more significant than 105 since it exceeded the prior swing high before reversing.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: Where buying pressure was, at least temporarily, exhausted. Does not by itself signal a reversal is happening; a swing high can form mid-uptrend as a normal pause. It only becomes significant compared to other swing highs or when later swept for liquidity (Module 4).

framework_placement.comes_before: Foundational -- nothing in the ICT framework needs to be understood before it.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into Higher High / Lower High classification, then Market Structure (Module 3), and later Buy-Side Liquidity (Module 4).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Marking every small wick as a swing high instead of applying the three-candle test consistently.
Treating a swing high as automatically bearish or as a guaranteed reversal signal.
Ignoring the timeframe: a swing high on a 1-minute chart and one on a weekly chart are not equally significant (Module 2).
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A swing high, on its own, is a structural label -- not a trade signal. It does not indicate direction, momentum, or intent until placed in context with the swing points before and after it and with higher-timeframe structure.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: A swing high on a 1-minute chart and a swing high on a weekly chart are not equally significant (see Module 2).
cited_sources_in_text: innercircletrader.net -- 'What is an ICT Swing Low? 3-Candle Formation Explained' (mirrored 3-candle swing-high test; accessed 2026).
innercircletrader.net -- 'What Is ICT Market Structure? BOS Highs, Lows & Liquidity' (STH/ITH/LTH hierarchy).
concepts.confidence_note: Book states: direct ICT primary-source video transcripts describing this specific three-candle rule by name were not available for direct verification; corroborated consistently across multiple independent ICT-focused tutorial sources and treated as reliable secondary documentation.

concepts.name: Swing Low
concepts.definition: A price point that is lower than the candles immediately surrounding it, marking a short-term turning point where downward movement paused or reversed.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: Mirror image of the swing high: a three-candle formation where the middle candle's low is lower than the low of the candle before it and after it. Organized into a hierarchy: Short-Term Low (STL), Intermediate-Term Low (ITL), Long-Term Low (LTL). A short-term low is promoted up the hierarchy when it proves significant enough to anchor a larger move (e.g., price reverses off it at a key level and breaks structure). ICT teaches price 'needs' to create these swing points to establish structure at all; without a confirmed swing low there is no reference point to judge whether a later low is higher (bullish) or lower (bearish).
detection_criteria: Find a candle whose low price is lower than the low of the candle immediately to its left.
Check that the same candle's low price is also lower than the low of the candle immediately to its right.
If both conditions are true, the middle candle qualifies as a swing low (an ICT Short-Term Low).
Record the exact price of that low as a reference level for structure and sell-side liquidity.
Repeat moving left to right to build a complete map of swing lows alongside swing highs.
preconditions: unspecified beyond the three-candle test itself
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 110 -> 104 -> 108 -> 101 -> 106. 104 is a swing low relative to 110 before it and 108 after it (a small dip). 101 is a lower, more significant swing low -- lower than 104, followed by a rise to 106; in ICT's hierarchy 101 carries more structural weight than 104 because it broke beneath the prior swing low.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: Where selling pressure was, at least temporarily, exhausted. Not inherently bullish or predictive; gains meaning only once compared against other swing points or later swept for liquidity.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Higher Low / Lower Low classification, Market Structure (Module 3), and Sell-Side Liquidity (Module 4).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Marking minor wicks as swing lows without applying the three-candle test consistently.
Assuming every swing low is a 'buy the dip' signal.
Comparing swing lows across different timeframes as if they were equally significant.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A swing low is a structural label describing where a short-term down-move stopped. It does not by itself indicate a bullish reversal is underway or that the level will hold on a future retest.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: unspecified in this section (see cross-timeframe caution in mistakes)
cited_sources_in_text: innercircletrader.net -- 'What is an ICT Swing Low? 3-Candle Formation Explained.'
innercircletrader.net -- 'What Is ICT Market Structure? BOS Highs, Lows & Liquidity' (STL/ITL/LTL hierarchy).
concepts.confidence_note: As with swing high, the precise three-candle rule is treated as reliable, well-corroborated secondary documentation rather than a confirmed direct ICT primary-source transcript quote.

concepts.name: Higher High
concepts.definition: A swing high that forms above the level of the previous swing high, showing that the upward move extended further than the prior one.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: One half of the definition of bullish market structure (the other half is higher lows). Some ICT-focused teaching adds a stricter qualification: a swing high only counts as a valid, structurally meaningful higher high after price has swept the liquidity resting just beyond the prior high or low (an 'inducement') on the way up. This refinement is flagged by the book as a documented community elaboration, not confirmed verbatim ICT phrasing.
detection_criteria: Identify two consecutive confirmed swing highs on the chart.
Compare their price levels.
If the more recent swing high is priced above the earlier one, label it a Higher High (HH).
Confirm this fits inside a broader sequence -- a single higher high in isolation is weaker evidence than several in a row combined with higher lows in between.
preconditions: Requires Swing High to already be understood/identified.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 105 -> 102 -> 108 -> 104 -> 112. First swing high 105; next swing high 108 is above 105 (HH); next swing high 112 is above 108 (another HH). The growing sequence 105 -> 108 -> 112 is evidence of bullish market structure, provided intervening swing lows are also rising.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: The most recent upward push exceeded the previous one -- one of the two required conditions for classifying the trend as bullish. Does not by itself confirm the uptrend will continue; it describes what already happened, not a forecast.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Swing High to already be understood.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into Trend and Bullish Market Structure (Module 3).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Calling a move a higher high after only one data point, without a confirmed prior swing high to compare against.
Ignoring higher lows and assuming higher highs alone define an uptrend.
Confusing a higher high on a lower timeframe with higher-timeframe structure (Module 2).
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A single higher high does not establish a trend. ICT's structural reading requires a consistent, ongoing sequence of higher highs and higher lows, and even then, structure can shift (Market Structure Shift, Module 3).
concepts.timeframe_relationship: unspecified beyond caution against confusing LTF higher high with HTF structure
cited_sources_in_text: litefinance.org -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Method' (HH/HL bullish structure definition).
chartinglens.com -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: The Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Concepts' (HH/HL, BOS/CHoCH framing).
concepts.confidence_note: The 'inducement sweep required to validate a higher high' refinement is explicitly labeled a community-level elaboration, not confirmed ICT verbatim phrasing.

concepts.name: Higher Low
concepts.definition: A swing low that forms above the level of the previous swing low, showing that the pullback did not retrace as far as the prior one.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: The second required ingredient (alongside higher high) for ICT's definition of bullish market structure; shows sellers were unable to push price back down to the previous low before buyers regained control. ICT-focused teaching describes higher lows as levels that should be 'protected' if the uptrend is genuinely intact -- price is generally not expected to close back below a confirmed higher low without calling the bullish structure into question.
detection_criteria: Identify two consecutive confirmed swing lows on the chart.
Compare their price levels.
If the more recent swing low is priced above the earlier one, label it a Higher Low (HL).
Check that this higher low sits between two rising swing highs -- this combination is what ICT reads as confirmed bullish structure.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 105 -> 102 -> 108 -> 104 -> 112. First swing low 102; next swing low 104 is above 102 (HL). Combined with higher highs (105 -> 108 -> 112), the full sequence 105/102, 108/104, 112 is a textbook bullish structure: every high exceeds the last, every low holds above the last.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: Demand returned before price reached the previous low, indicating a relatively shallow pullback. Does not guarantee price will not eventually break below it; describes the current structural picture only.
common_pairings: Order Block / Fair Value Gap (as the origin of the bounce)

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into Trend and Bullish Market Structure (Module 3).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Assuming any bounce is a higher low without confirming it against the prior swing low.
Ignoring a break below a prior confirmed higher low, which ICT reads as an early warning that bullish structure may be ending.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A higher low is descriptive of price that has already happened. It becomes structurally important only in combination with higher highs, and can be invalidated by a later break below it.
cited_sources_in_text: litefinance.org -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Method.'
innercircletrader.net -- 'Higher High and Higher Low -- Bullish Market Structure Identification.'

concepts.name: Lower High
concepts.definition: A swing high that forms below the level of the previous swing high, showing that the upward push failed to reach as far as the prior one.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: One of two required conditions (with lower low) for ICT's definition of bearish market structure; shows buyers were unable to push price back up to the previous high before sellers regained control. A lower high forming after higher highs/higher lows is one of the earliest structural clues for a possible bearish shift -- though ICT is explicit that a shift is only confirmed once price actually breaks a prior structural low (Market Structure Shift, Module 3), not merely because one lower high appeared.
detection_criteria: Identify two consecutive confirmed swing highs.
Compare their price levels.
If the more recent swing high is priced below the earlier one, label it a Lower High (LH).
Check whether it is paired with a lower low -- that combination confirms bearish structure rather than a single failed push.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 112 -> 106 -> 109 -> 101 -> 104. First swing high 112; next swing high 109 fails to exceed 112 (LH). This single lower high is a caution flag but not yet confirmation of a bearish trend without a lower low too.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: The most recent upward push was weaker than the prior one -- a potential early sign that upward momentum is fading. Does not by itself confirm a trend reversal or bearish bias.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Trend and Bearish Market Structure (Module 3).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Treating one lower high as proof the trend has reversed.
Ignoring the higher-timeframe context when a lower high appears only on a lower timeframe (Module 2).
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A lower high describes a single failed push higher. It is a caution signal at most, not a stand-alone bearish trade trigger.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: Caution against confusing an LTF-only lower high with HTF context (Module 2).
cited_sources_in_text: chartinglens.com -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: The Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Concepts' (LH/LL bearish structure definition).

concepts.name: Lower Low
concepts.definition: A swing low that forms below the level of the previous swing low, showing that the downward move extended further than the prior one.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: The second required condition (with lower high) for ICT's definition of bearish market structure; confirms sellers pushed price beyond the previous floor. A confirmed break below a prior structural low (producing a lower low) is treated as stronger structural evidence of bearish control than a lower high alone, because it represents an actual break of a defended level rather than just a weaker rally.
detection_criteria: Identify two consecutive confirmed swing lows.
Compare their price levels.
If the more recent swing low is priced below the earlier one, label it a Lower Low (LL).
Confirm this sits alongside a lower high -- together they confirm bearish structure.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 112 -> 106 -> 109 -> 101 -> 104. First swing low 106; next swing low 101 is below 106 (LL). Combined with the lower high (109, below 112), the full picture 112/109 and 106/101 is a textbook bearish structure.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: The most recent downward push exceeded the prior one, satisfying (with a lower high) ICT's definition of bearish structure. Describes what already happened; does not guarantee further downside.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Trend and Bearish Market Structure (Module 3).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Assuming a lower low always means 'sell now' rather than checking the broader higher-timeframe context.
Missing that a lower low can also be a liquidity sweep that gets reversed (Module 4) rather than a genuine continuation.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A lower low can mean genuine bearish continuation, or price dipping below an old low specifically to collect resting liquidity before reversing. Distinguishing the two requires Module 4/5 concepts (displacement and liquidity sweeps).
cited_sources_in_text: chartinglens.com -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: The Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Concepts.'
litefinance.org -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Method.'

concepts.name: Trend
concepts.definition: The general direction in which price is moving over a given period, expressed structurally as a sustained sequence of higher highs and higher lows (uptrend) or lower highs and lower lows (downtrend).
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: ICT does not treat trend as a separate indicator-based concept; it is a direct output of market structure. Uptrend = continues printing higher highs and higher lows; downtrend = continues printing lower highs and lower lows. When neither pattern holds consistently, the market is range-bound/structurally undecided. Because ICT reads structure on multiple timeframes at once (Module 2), a market can be in an uptrend on one timeframe while in a downtrend/retracement on another -- trends are fractal.
detection_criteria: Map out a series of swing highs and swing lows across the chart.
Check whether the highs and lows are both rising (higher highs and higher lows) -- if so, bullish (up) trend.
Check whether the highs and lows are both falling (lower highs and lower lows) -- if so, bearish (down) trend.
If highs and lows are not consistently rising or falling together, treat the market as range-bound rather than trending.
Repeat this check on a higher timeframe to see whether the lower-timeframe trend agrees with or contradicts the larger picture (Module 2).
preconditions: Requires Higher High, Higher Low, Lower High, and Lower Low.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 105 -> 102 -> 108 -> 104 -> 112 -> 107. Swing highs 105, 108, 112 each higher than the last; swing lows 102, 104 each higher than the last. Both highs and lows rising describes an uptrend, up to the final pullback to 107 which has not yet broken the pattern.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: The direction that has been structurally dominant so far; feeds directly into bias (Module 10). Does not tell the trader when the current move will end -- a trend is treated as valid until structure actually shifts (Module 3), not based on a feeling it has 'gone on too long.'

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Higher High, Higher Low, Lower High, and Lower Low.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Retracement, Market Structure (Module 3), and ultimately Bias (Module 10).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Declaring a trend based on only two candles instead of a genuine sequence of confirmed swing points.
Ignoring the timeframe being viewed and assuming the trend on a 5-minute chart applies to the daily chart.
Treating a single retracement against the trend as proof the trend has reversed.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A trend is only assumed to remain intact while structure continues to confirm it. The moment structure breaks in the opposing direction, the trend classification must be reassessed (Market Structure Shift, Module 3) -- trend is not assumed to persist indefinitely by default.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: Trends are fractal across timeframes; a market can trend up on one timeframe while trending down or retracing on another (Module 2).
cited_sources_in_text: fxopen.com -- 'ICT Concepts: What Is Inner Circle Trading?' (fractal, multi-timeframe nature of trend/structure).
litefinance.org -- 'ICT Trading Strategy: Complete Guide to Inner Circle Trader Method.'

concepts.name: Retracement
concepts.definition: A temporary price move against the prevailing trend that does not break the trend's structure, before price resumes in the original trend direction.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: The pullback phase that produces the higher low (in an uptrend) or the lower high (in a downtrend); a necessary, expected part of trending price delivery, not a warning sign by itself. ICT's price-delivery model (developed further in Module 7's OTE and Module 9's Power of 3) treats retracements as opportunities: a disciplined trader waits for the retracement into a specific zone rather than chasing price at the extreme of the prior move.
detection_criteria: Confirm an established trend using swing highs and lows.
Watch for a move in the opposite direction of that trend.

Confirm that this opposite move does not break the most recent confirmed swing point against the trend (e.g., in an uptrend, the pullback should not close below the last confirmed higher low's originating structure).
If the trend resumes afterward, the move is classified as a retracement rather than a reversal.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 108 -> 104 -> 114. Price rises 100 to 108 (trend move), pulls back to 104 (retracement), then rises to 114 (trend resuming, new higher high). Because price did not fall to/below 100 and the uptrend resumed, the pullback to 104 is read as a retracement rather than a reversal.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: Price is offering a temporary discount (in an uptrend) or premium (in a downtrend) relative to the recent extreme -- the basic logic behind waiting for a retracement before entering in the trend direction. Does not tell the trader in advance how deep the pullback will go, or guarantee the trend will resume -- a retracement can also turn into a full reversal, which is why Market Structure Shift (Module 3) exists to distinguish the two after the fact.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Fibonacci/OTE (Module 7) and, combined with liquidity and displacement concepts, into the ICT Buy/Sell Models (Modules 11-12).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Entering a trade the instant a retracement begins, without waiting for confirmation that it is a retracement rather than a reversal.
Assuming every retracement will reach a specific, fixed percentage of the prior move.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A retracement is only confirmed as a retracement in hindsight, once the trend resumes. While happening, it cannot be distinguished with certainty from the start of a genuine reversal -- this is why ICT's framework pairs retracement analysis with structure, liquidity, and displacement concepts rather than treating a pullback alone as a signal.
cited_sources_in_text: General ICT price-delivery framing corroborated across litefinance.org and chartinglens.com ICT strategy guides.
concepts.confidence_note: ICT's own specific terminology for 'retracement' as a standalone named concept (versus only within Fibonacci/OTE) was not directly verifiable from primary transcripts; treated as inferred/corroborated, not directly quoted ICT definition.

concepts.name: Key Support Levels
concepts.definition: A price area where prior demand was strong enough to stop or reverse a decline, typically marked by an old swing low, and which price is expected to react to again if revisited.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: ICT-focused teaching frames support/resistance as concrete evidence of resting liquidity and unfilled institutional interest rather than abstract lines. Sell-stop orders and unfilled buy orders are taught to cluster below/around old lows, affecting price behavior on return. ICT's broader 'key levels' framework extends support to prior day/week/month lows, session lows, and the lower boundary of an equilibrium range -- all reference points price is likely to react to or seek out.
detection_criteria: Locate a confirmed swing low, prior day/week/month low, or session low on the chart.
Mark the exact price of that low as a reference level.
Note whether price has reacted (bounced) from that specific price area more than once -- repeated reactions increase, but do not guarantee, significance.
Watch how price behaves when it returns to that level in future: a clean reaction, a sweep-and-reverse, or a break through it (Modules 4-6).
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 95 -> 102 -> 96 -> 108. Price drops to 95 and bounces (first test). Price later drops to 96 (close to but not exactly 95) and bounces again toward 108. The 95-96 zone has reacted twice, marked as a key support area worth continuing to watch.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: A price zone where downward moves have previously been rejected -- useful context for anticipating where a decline might slow or reverse. Does not tell the trader the level will hold next time; ICT's framework treats an old low as more likely to attract price (as a liquidity target) than to be an unbreakable floor forever.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Liquidity (Module 4) and PD Arrays (Module 6), where the same zone is analyzed for Order Blocks and Fair Value Gaps.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Treating support as a precise single price rather than a zone.
Assuming support will always hold, rather than recognizing it may first be swept for liquidity before reversing, or broken outright.
Drawing support levels on every minor wick instead of focusing on levels with real structural or liquidity significance.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A key support level describes historical price behavior, not a guarantee of future behavior. Within ICT's framework, an old low is as likely to be treated as a magnet for a liquidity sweep as it is to be a level that holds cleanly -- resolved using liquidity and displacement concepts (Modules 4-5), not by the support level alone.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: unspecified (references prior day/week/month lows and session lows as multi-scale key levels)
cited_sources_in_text: chartinglens.com -- 'Support and Resistance Levels: Complete Trading Guide.'
TradingView ICT key-level tool documentation ('ict key level Pro++', 'Key Levels ICT').
concepts.confidence_note: Cited tooling/indicator descriptions are community-built implementations, not ICT's own primary material; used only to corroborate which levels ICT-style traders treat as key.

concepts.name: Key Resistance Levels
concepts.definition: A price area where prior selling pressure was strong enough to stop or reverse a rally, typically marked by an old swing high, and which price is expected to react to again if revisited.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning: Mirror of key support. Buy-stop orders and unfilled sell orders are understood to cluster above/around old highs -- directly relevant to ICT's liquidity framework (Module 4). ICT's key-levels framework extends resistance to prior day/week/month highs, session highs, and the upper boundary of an equilibrium range.
detection_criteria: Locate a confirmed swing high, prior day/week/month high, or session high on the chart.
Mark the exact price of that high as a reference level.
Note whether price has reacted (turned down) from that specific area more than once.
Watch how price behaves on a future return to that level -- a clean rejection, a sweep-and-reverse, or a break through (Modules 4-6).
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example: 100 -> 108 -> 103 -> 107 -> 96. Price rises to 108 and turns down (first test). Price later rises to 107 (close to but not exactly 108) and turns down again toward 96. The 107-108 zone has reacted twice, marking it as a key resistance area.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader: A price zone where upward moves have previously been rejected -- useful context for anticipating where a rally might slow or reverse. Does not guarantee the level will hold on the next approach; ICT's framework treats an old high as a likely liquidity target (buy-side liquidity resting above it) as much as a ceiling.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into Liquidity (Module 4) and PD Arrays (Module 6).

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Treating resistance as one exact price instead of a zone.
Assuming resistance will always hold rather than first being swept for liquidity.
Marking too many minor highs as 'key' resistance, diluting the significance of genuinely important levels.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: A key resistance level describes historical behavior, not a guarantee. Whether an old high holds, gets swept, or is broken outright depends on the liquidity and displacement concepts covered next, not on the level in isolation.
concepts.timeframe_relationship: unspecified (references prior day/week/month highs and session highs as multi-scale key levels)
cited_sources_in_text: chartinglens.com -- 'Support and Resistance Levels: Complete Trading Guide.'
concepts.confidence_note: Cited tooling descriptions are community implementations used only to corroborate which levels are treated as key within ICT-style analysis.

relationships.statement: The ten concepts in this module form a single continuous logical chain: Swing High and Swing Low are the two atomic building blocks of price structure. They are compared against immediate predecessors to classify Higher High/Higher Low/Lower High/Lower Low; these classifications are the direct evidence used to determine Trend (a consistent run of HH+HL = uptrend; a consistent run of LH+LL = downtrend). Once a trend is established, Retracement describes expected pullbacks within it -- the same pullbacks that produce the higher lows (uptrend) or lower highs (downtrend) used to confirm the trend, forming a closed loop (trend produces retracements; retracements produce the swing points that confirm trend). When a swing high or swing low proves durable (price returns and reacts again), it graduates into a Key Support or Resistance level, which the rest of the ICT framework (starting with Liquidity in Module 4) treats as significant.

contradictions_or_ambiguities.description: The book repeatedly flags that the precise 'three-candle test' for swing highs/lows, and the 'inducement sweep required to validate a higher high' refinement, could not be directly verified from ICT primary-source transcripts and are instead community-level/secondary-source corroborated. This is a source-authority hedge rather than a content contradiction, but it means these mechanical definitions are ICT-adjacent/community-standard rather than confirmed verbatim ICT doctrine.

passage_a.text: Direct ICT primary-source video transcripts describing this specific three-candle rule by name were not available for direct verification in this research pass...

passage_b.text: The 'inducement sweep required to validate a higher high' refinement is a community-level elaboration documented on ICT-focused tutorial sites, not confirmed here as ICT's own verbatim phrasing.

common_misconceptions: Believing every wick on a chart is a meaningful swing point rather than applying a consistent identification test.
Believing a trend is defined by 'the general feeling' of the chart rather than by a specific sequence of swing-point comparisons.
Believing support and resistance levels are guaranteed to hold, rather than being historical reference points that may be swept for liquidity or broken outright.
Believing a retracement can be identified with certainty while it is still happening, rather than only in hindsight once the trend resumes or fails to resume.
self_test_questions: What two conditions must both be true for a candle's high to qualify as a swing high?
What is the difference between a higher high and a lower high?
Can a single higher high, on its own, confirm an uptrend? Why or why not?
What distinguishes a retracement from a reversal, and why can that distinction only be confirmed after the fact?
Why does ICT's framework treat an old support or resistance level as a potential liquidity target rather than a guaranteed floor or ceiling?

module_review_notes.practical_chart_exercise: Using the sequence 50 -> 62 -> 55 -> 70 -> 58 -> 78 -> 65, identify every swing high and swing low using the three-candle logic taught in this module, classify each swing high as higher or lower relative to the one before it, classify each swing low the same way, state whether this sequence represents an uptrend, a downtrend, or a range, and identify the single retracement in the sequence that does not break the pattern.
